blocks.text: A 52-year-old man collapses at the end of a five-a-side football match. He is unresponsive and gasping slowly. Within the first two minutes, what the bystanders do matters more than any drug the ambulance will later carry.

blocks.markdown: **Cardiac arrest** is the sudden cessation of effective mechanical heart action, so there is no circulation to the brain. Brain injury begins within minutes, which is why resuscitation is a *sequence* in which every delay costs outcome. The UK framework (Resuscitation Council UK, RCUK) divides the response into **basic life support (BLS)**, which needs no equipment beyond a defibrillator, and **advanced life support (ALS)**, which adds a monitor/defibrillator, airway adjuncts, drugs and a search for causes.

blocks.title: Shockable versus non-shockable rhythms
blocks.text: Shockable rhythms are ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT): chaotic or rapid ventricular activity that can be terminated by a defibrillation shock. Non-shockable rhythms are pulseless electrical activity (PEA; organised electrical activity but no palpable pulse) and asystole (no electrical activity). A shock does nothing to a heart in PEA or asystole.

items: Make sure it is safe to approach. Check for a response: gently shake the shoulders and ask loudly whether the person is all right.

If there is no response, shout for help, open the airway (head tilt and chin lift) and look, listen and feel for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds. Occasional gasps (agonal breathing) are not normal breathing.
If breathing is absent or not normal, call the emergency number (999 in the UK) and send someone to fetch an automated external defibrillator (AED). Treat as cardiac arrest.

Start chest compressions in the centre of the chest, hands one on top of the other, depth about 5 to 6 cm, rate 100 to 120 per minute, allowing full recoil. Give 30 compressions then 2 rescue breaths if trained and willing, otherwise continue compressions.
As soon as the AED arrives, switch it on and follow its voice prompts, attaching the pads as shown. Minimise every pause in compressions.

blocks.title: Check current guidance
blocks.text: Depths, rates, compression:ventilation ratios, energies and drug doses quoted here follow the Resuscitation Council UK adult algorithms as generally taught. They are updated periodically; check against current RCUK, NICE and local guidance before using any figure clinically.

blocks.markdown: **Why defibrillation is time critical.** In VF the chance of a successful shock falls with every minute without one. CPR buys time by supplying a trickle of coronary and cerebral perfusion, but only a shock can restore an organised rhythm. A public-access AED analyses the rhythm itself: it will advise a shock only for VF or pVT, so a lay rescuer cannot harm a person with a perfusing rhythm. After a shock, resume CPR immediately without checking for a pulse, and continue for two minutes before the rhythm is reassessed.

blocks.title: Following the shockable pathway in a monitored VF arrest
blocks.prompt: A monitored 60-year-old on the coronary care unit collapses and the monitor shows VF. The patient is pulseless. Describe the actions at time 0, 2 and 4 minutes, and when adrenaline and amiodarone are given.

steps.text: Time 0: confirm unresponsive and not breathing normally, call the resuscitation team, start 30:2 compressions while the defibrillator pads or paddles are applied. Charge during compressions and give the first shock with a minimal pause (RCUK: initial biphasic energy about 150 to 200 J, check the device and local protocol).
Immediately after shock 1, restart CPR for 2 minutes without a pulse check. Secure IV or intraosseous (IO) access and begin looking for reversible causes.
Time 2 minutes: pause briefly for a rhythm check. VF persists, so deliver shock 2 and resume CPR at once. Consider an airway adjunct while keeping compressions going.

Time 4 minutes: VF persists again, so give shock 3 and resume CPR. After the third shock, RCUK teaches adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO and amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO (check doses against current guidance). A further amiodarone 150 mg is given after the fifth shock if VF/pVT persists (RCUK; check current guideline). Adrenaline is then repeated every 3 to 5 minutes, alternate cycles.

Continue cycles of 2 minutes CPR then rhythm check until ROSC (return of spontaneous circulation) or the decision to stop. If an organised rhythm appears with signs of life or a pulse, move to post-resuscitation care.

blocks.answer: Shock at 0, 2 and 4 minutes with 2-minute CPR cycles between; adrenaline 1 mg and amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock, with a further amiodarone 150 mg after the fifth shock (verify against current RCUK doses), then continue cycles while seeking reversible causes.

rows: As soon as IV/IO access is achieved
As soon as IV/IO access is achieved
blocks.caption: Rhythm-based treatment (doses to be checked against current RCUK guidance)

blocks.markdown: **Non-shockable rhythms.** The treatment of PEA and asystole is high-quality CPR, early adrenaline and, above all, the hunt for a **reversible cause**. In PEA there is organised electrical activity but the heart is not generating a pulse, often because of a mechanical or physiological problem outside the myocardium. If a rhythm that looks like asystole is suspected, confirm it: check lead connection, gain and a second lead. A very slow organised rhythm with no pulse is PEA, not asystole.

blocks.title: Reversible causes: the 4 Hs and 4 Ts
blocks.text: Hypoxia; Hypovolaemia; Hyper-/hypokalaemia and other metabolic disturbances; Hypo-/hyperthermia. Tension pneumothorax; Tamponade (cardiac); Toxins; Thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary). Searching for these in every arrest, especially PEA, is part of ALS.

blocks.title: PEA arrest in a young asthmatic
blocks.prompt: A 24-year-old with severe acute asthma becomes unresponsive in the resuscitation room. The monitor shows organised complexes at 120 per minute but there is no pulse. Reason through treatment.

steps.text: Organised rhythm with no pulse means PEA, a non-shockable rhythm. Start CPR 30:2 and give adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO as soon as access is gained (check dose against current RCUK guidance). Do not defibrillate.

Ask which reversible cause fits the story: profound hypoxia from bronchospasm is the leading Hypoxia cause; a tension pneumothorax (barotrauma, or complication of positive-pressure ventilation) is the leading Tension pneumothorax cause.

Oxygenate and secure the airway with the most skilled operator available. Look for asymmetrical chest movement and absent breath sounds; if a tension pneumothorax is suspected, decompress immediately (needle or finger thoracostomy per local protocol) rather than waiting for imaging.
Continue 2-minute cycles, re-assess for other causes such as hypovolaemia or hyperkalaemia (point-of-care blood gas), and treat what is found.

blocks.answer: PEA from hypoxia and/or tension pneumothorax: CPR, adrenaline, oxygenation, decompress the chest if tension is suspected; do not shock.

blocks.title: What examiners look for
blocks.text: Name the rhythm first, then state whether it is shockable, then give the sequence. Always mention minimising pauses, a 2-minute cycle length and a systematic search for 4 Hs and 4 Ts.

items: High-quality compressions: correct depth and rate, full recoil, minimal interruption.
Early defibrillation when VF/pVT is present; the AED is safe for lay use.
Airway and ventilation: bag-mask initially, advanced airway only if it does not interrupt compressions.
Drugs support CPR and defibrillation; they never replace them.
After ROSC, move to post-resuscitation care with an ABCDE approach and identify the cause.

points: BLS: check response and breathing, call for help and an AED, start 30:2 compressions, attach the AED and follow its prompts.
Shockable rhythms (VF, pVT) need a shock then 2 minutes of CPR; adrenaline and amiodarone are given after the third shock (check current doses).
Non-shockable rhythms (PEA, asystole) are treated with CPR, early adrenaline and search for reversible causes.
The 4 Hs and 4 Ts are systematically sought and treated in every arrest.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman collapses in a shopping centre queue. A bystander finds her unresponsive; after opening her airway she is not breathing normally. What is the most appropriate next action?

options.text: Call the emergency number, send for an AED and start chest compressions
Check for a carotid pulse for 30 seconds before deciding what to do
Place her in the recovery position and wait for the ambulance
Give 2 minutes of rescue breaths before calling for help

questions.correctOptionText: Call the emergency number, send for an AED and start chest compressions

distractorRationale.a: Correct: absent or abnormal breathing in an unresponsive adult is cardiac arrest, so call, get an AED and start compressions.
distractorRationale.b: Pulse checks by lay rescuers are unreliable and delay compressions.
distractorRationale.c: The recovery position is for unresponsive people who are breathing normally.
distractorRationale.d: Compressions and early defibrillation take priority over rescue breaths in an adult collapse.

questions.explanation: Unresponsiveness with absent or abnormal breathing is treated as cardiac arrest. The priorities are to summon help and an AED and to begin compressions immediately, because circulation is absent and delay in perfusion and defibrillation worsens outcome.

questions.stem: During a witnessed arrest the monitor shows a chaotic, irregular waveform of varying amplitude with no identifiable QRS complexes. There is no pulse. What is the correct immediate treatment?

options.text: Defibrillate as soon as possible, then resume CPR for 2 minutes
Give adrenaline and continue CPR without a shock
Perform synchronised cardioversion
Give atropine for bradycardia

questions.correctOptionText: Defibrillate as soon as possible, then resume CPR for 2 minutes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is ventricular fibrillation, a shockable rhythm; shock then CPR.
distractorRationale.b: Adrenaline first is the pathway for non-shockable rhythms; in VF a shock comes first.
distractorRationale.c: Synchronised cardioversion needs identifiable QRS complexes to synchronise with; VF has none and is defibrillated.
distractorRationale.d: Atropine is not used for VF and is no longer part of the cardiac arrest algorithm.

questions.explanation: A chaotic waveform without QRS complexes in a pulseless patient is VF. VF is shockable, so the patient should be defibrillated immediately and CPR resumed straight away for 2 minutes.

questions.stem: An unresponsive 45-year-old with no pulse has organised QRS complexes at 38 per minute on the monitor. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: This is PEA; give CPR and early adrenaline and look for reversible causes, with no shock
This is asystole; confirm by checking lead connections
This is pulseless VT; shock immediately
This is a perfusing bradycardia; give atropine only

questions.correctOptionText: This is PEA; give CPR and early adrenaline and look for reversible causes, with no shock

distractorRationale.a: Correct: organised electrical activity with no pulse is PEA, which is not shocked.
distractorRationale.b: Asystole means no electrical activity; this trace has organised complexes.
distractorRationale.c: VT is a fast wide-complex rhythm; a slow organised rhythm is not pVT.
distractorRationale.d: The patient is pulseless, so this is not a perfusing rhythm.

questions.explanation: Pulseless patients with organised electrical activity are in PEA regardless of rate. Defibrillation does not help PEA, so treatment is high-quality CPR, adrenaline and a search for the 4 Hs and 4 Ts.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man, day 3 after total hip replacement, collapses suddenly after sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. He is pulseless with PEA. He has a swollen, tender right calf and distended neck veins; breath sounds are equal. Which reversible cause is most likely?

options.text: Thrombosis (massive pulmonary embolism)
Tension pneumothorax
Hypovolaemia from wound bleeding
Hypothermia

distractorRationale.a: Correct: recent surgery, calf swelling, pleuritic pain, breathlessness and raised venous pressure point to massive PE.
distractorRationale.b: Tension pneumothorax would typically give unequal breath sounds and tracheal deviation; breath sounds are equal here.
distractorRationale.c: Hypovolaemia would give flat, not distended, neck veins.
distractorRationale.d: There is nothing in the history to suggest hypothermia.

questions.explanation: The risk factor (postoperative immobility), the calf signs and the equal breath sounds with raised venous pressure favour pulmonary embolism, a thrombotic cause. Where PE is suspected as the cause of arrest, thrombolysis may be considered with prolonged CPR according to current guidance.

questions.stem: A lay rescuer attaches an AED to an unresponsive man. The device analyses and announces: 'No shock advised. Resume CPR.' What should the rescuer do?

options.text: Resume chest compressions immediately and continue until the AED prompts reanalysis
Remove the pads because the man must have a pulse
Press the shock button to override the prompt
Stop CPR and check for a pulse for 1 minute

questions.correctOptionText: Resume chest compressions immediately and continue until the AED prompts reanalysis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: no shock advised does not mean the patient has a pulse; the rhythm is non-shockable, so CPR continues.
distractorRationale.b: A non-shockable rhythm may be PEA or asystole, so a pulse cannot be assumed.
distractorRationale.c: Most AEDs will not shock unless a shockable rhythm is found, and a shock would not help a non-shockable rhythm.
distractorRationale.d: Prolonged pulse checks interrupt compressions without benefit.

questions.explanation: An AED that advises no shock has detected a non-shockable rhythm or none that would respond to shock; it does not mean the circulation has returned. CPR must continue without interruption until the device prompts again or the patient shows signs of life.

questions.stem: A rescuer delivers cycles of 30 compressions at a rate of 110 per minute, followed by a pause of 5 seconds in which 2 rescue breaths are given, and then immediately repeats. Calculate the average number of compressions actually delivered per minute over many cycles. Give your answer in compressions per minute, to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: Thirty compressions at 110 per minute take 30/110 of a minute, which is 16.4 s. Adding the 5 s breath pause gives 21.4 s per cycle, so the delivered rate is 30/21.4 x 60 which is about 84 per minute. The interruptions for breaths therefore reduce delivered compressions well below the nominal rate, which is why pauses must be kept short.

questions.stem: During one 2-minute CPR cycle (120 s) in a hospital arrest, compressions are paused for a 9 s rhythm check, a 5 s pause for the shock and a 6 s pause to place an airway. No other pauses occur. Calculate the chest compression fraction (time spent compressing as a percentage of the cycle). Give your answer as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Total pause time is 9 + 5 + 6 = 20 s, so compression time is 120 - 20 = 100 s. The fraction is 100/120 = 0.833, or 83.3 per cent. Higher compression fractions are associated with better perfusion, so teams aim to minimise pre- and post-shock pauses.

questions.stem: Compare the treatment of a pulseless patient found in VF with one found in PEA, and explain why the two pathways differ. Include the role of drugs and of reversible causes. (Doses should be checked against current RCUK guidance.)
markingGuide: VF is shockable because chaotic ventricular activity can be terminated by defibrillation, restoring an organised rhythm.
PEA has organised electrical activity but no output; a shock does not treat the underlying problem so it is non-shockable.
VF pathway: shock, 2 minutes CPR, repeat; adrenaline and amiodarone given after the third shock.
PEA pathway: immediate high-quality CPR with adrenaline as soon as access is available, continued in 2-minute cycles.
Both pathways require a systematic search for the 4 Hs and 4 Ts, which is especially important in PEA.
Mentions checking doses and energies against current guidance.
questions.explanation: The pathways differ because defibrillation corrects only a disordered electrical rhythm. In PEA the failure is usually mechanical or physiological, so treatment relies on CPR, adrenaline and correction of the cause.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is in cardiac arrest after being pulled from a house fire and the monitor shows PEA. List the reversible causes (4 Hs and 4 Ts) and explain how you would decide which are most relevant here.
markingGuide: Lists the 4 Hs: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hyper-/hypokalaemia and metabolic, hypo-/hyperthermia.
Lists the 4 Ts: tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis.
Identifies hypoxia (smoke inhalation, airway burns) as a leading cause and toxins (carbon monoxide, cyanide) as relevant to the history.
Uses history, examination and bedside tests (blood gas, ultrasound) to confirm or exclude causes.
States that identified causes are treated while CPR continues, for example securing the airway and giving 100 per cent oxygen.
questions.explanation: Reversible causes are sought in all arrests but the history prioritises them. Smoke exposure makes hypoxia and toxins most likely, and treatment targets these while CPR continues.

questions.stem: True or false: hypokalaemia and hyperkalaemia are both considered reversible causes of cardiac arrest in the 4 Hs group.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The 'H' for electrolytes covers both hyper- and hypokalaemia and other metabolic disturbances, including calcium and magnesium disorders. Both can cause malignant arrhythmias and are corrected as part of the search for reversible causes.
